questions.q: What is the real difference between qualitative and quantitative risk assessment, according to this lesson?
options: Quantitative assessment is only used by auditors, while qualitative is only used by engineers
There is no real difference — they produce the same ranking, just in different formats
They answer two different questions: qualitative ranks a backlog for triage, quantitative justifies a specific spend decision in dollars
Qualitative assessment is always more accurate because it involves more people
questions.explain: Qualitative assessment answers "what should we work on first?" Quantitative assessment answers "is this risk worth spending this much money to reduce?" They are built for different decisions, not different difficulty levels of the same task.

questions.q: Why can't you meaningfully compare a "High" risk from one team's register to a "High" risk from a different team's register?
options: Because High/Medium/Low labels are randomly assigned by software
Because only quantitative scores are allowed to appear on a risk register
Because ISO 31000 prohibits cross-team comparison of qualitative labels
Because the labels are subjective and scored by different people against different internal reference points, not a common unit
questions.explain: Qualitative labels aren't denominated in any shared unit. "High" means something different depending on who scored it and what they've personally seen fail, which is fine for ranking one team's own backlog but breaks down across teams.

questions.q: How does quantitative risk assessment typically express a risk's severity?
options: As an estimated annual dollar loss exposure, often given as a range rather than one number
As a single word: High, Medium, or Low
As a color on a five-by-five matrix
As a percentage of the company's total annual revenue, fixed by regulation
questions.explain: Quantitative assessment replaces category labels with a dollar figure — commonly a range of expected annual loss, like "$400,000 to $2.1 million, median around $900,000" — which lets unrelated risks be compared directly.

questions.q: In practice, when do organizations typically reach for quantitative risk assessment instead of qualitative scoring?
options: For every item on the risk register, every single quarter, with no exceptions
For decisions big enough to justify the extra work — a major insurance renewal, a board's dollar-figure question, or an expensive control buy-vs-build call
Only when no qualitative data exists at all
Never — quantitative methods are described in this lesson as obsolete
questions.explain: Quantitative assessment takes real time and data, so it gets reserved for high-stakes decisions, while qualitative scoring remains the default, continuous lens for the whole backlog.

questions.q: What is the workable pattern this lesson describes for running qualitative and quantitative assessment together?
options: Quantitative assessment replaces qualitative scoring entirely once an organization matures
They must always be run by two completely separate, non-communicating teams
Qualitative scoring narrows a large register down to a short list, then quantitative analysis is run on just that short list before money is committed
Qualitative scoring is only valid after a quantitative figure has already been calculated
questions.explain: The cheap qualitative pass narrows 200 risks down to a handful; the expensive, defensible quantitative pass is then reserved for deciding what those few risks are actually worth addressing.
